Problem 1 - Tidyverse: New Zealand

a.
```{r}
nzge <- nzge
head(nzge)

#help(nzge)

vote_count <- nzge |>
  group_by(election_year, voting_type) |>
  summarize(num_votes = sum(votes)) |>
  arrange(num_votes) |>
  ungroup() |>
  rename(
    "Election Year" = election_year,
    "Voting Type" = voting_type,
    "Total Vote Count" = num_votes
  ) 
vote_count
```

b.
```{r}
#proportion of votes for each party in 2014 Candidate election
  #sorted by percent of vote
party_props <- nzge |>
  filter(election_year == 2014 & voting_type == "Candidate") |>
  group_by(party) |>
  summarize(num_votes = sum(votes)) |>
  mutate(vote_prop = num_votes / sum(num_votes)) |>
  arrange(desc(vote_prop)) |>
  ungroup() |>
    rename(
    "Party" = party,
    "Number of Votes" = num_votes,
    "Proportion of Total Votes" = vote_prop
  )
party_props
```

c.
```{r}
winning_party <- nzge |>
  group_by(election_year, voting_type, party) |>
  summarize(num_votes = sum(votes)) |>
  slice_max(order_by = num_votes, n = 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  #just show year + winner
  select(-num_votes) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = voting_type, values_from = party) |>
  rename(
    "Election Year" = election_year,
    "Candidate Vote Winner" = Candidate,
    "Party Vote Winner" = Party
  )
winning_party
```

Problem 2 - Tidyverse: Tennis

Your answers should show both the output from R that allows you to answer it, 
as well as a written answer.

Referenced matches_data_dictionary.txt for variable names
```{r}
atp <- read.csv("atp_matches_2019.csv")
head(atp)
```

a. How many tournaments took place in 2019?
```{r}
#https://www.statology.org/dplyr-count-distinct/ for idea
num_tournaments_2019 <- atp |>
  summarize("Number of tournaments" = n_distinct(tourney_id))
num_tournaments_2019
```

128 tournaments took place in 2019. 

b. Did any player win more than one tournament? 
If so, how many players won more than one tournament, and how many tournaments 
did the most winning player(s) win?
```{r}
tournament_wins <- atp |>
  #based on documentation in github, F should be the final round
    #of a tournament -> winner should be tournament winner
  filter(round == "F") |>
  group_by(winner_name) |>
  #reminder: n() counts num rows in each group
  summarize(tournaments_won = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(tournaments_won)) |>
  ungroup()
tournament_wins

more_than_one <- tournament_wins |>
  filter(tournaments_won > 1)
more_than_one

most_wins <- more_than_one |> 
  slice_max(order_by = tournaments_won, with_ties = TRUE)
most_wins
```

Yes, 12 players won more than one tournament. The players that won the most 
tournaments both won 5 (Dominic Thiem and Novak Djokovic). 

c. Is there any evidence that winners have more aces than losers? 
(If you address this with a hypothesis test, do not use base R functionality - 
continue to remain in the Tidyverse.)
```{r}
aces_test <- atp |>
  mutate(num_aces_diff  = w_ace - l_ace) |>
  t_test(response = num_aces_diff, mu = 0, alternative = "greater")
aces_test
```

The very small p-value (1.53e-34) means we reject the null that the difference 
between the number of winners' aces and losers' aces is 0. On average, it 
appears that winners have about 1.705 more aces than losers. 

d. Identify the player(s) with the highest win-rate. 
(Note that this is NOT asking for the highest number of wins.) 
Restrict to players with at least 5 matches.

```{r}
#get number of matches won for each player
matches_won <- atp |>
  group_by(winner_name) |>
  summarize(matches_won = n()) |>
  arrange(matches_won) |>
  #for joining later
  rename(player_name = winner_name) |> 
  ungroup()
head(matches_won)

#get num of matches lost for each player
matches_lost <- atp |>
  group_by(loser_name) |>
  summarize(matches_lost = n()) |>
  arrange(matches_lost) |>
  rename(player_name = loser_name) |> 
  ungroup()
head(matches_lost)

#join to get all the players' matches in one df
total_matches <- left_join(matches_won, matches_lost, by = "player_name") |>
  mutate(
    total_matches = matches_won + matches_lost,
    win_rate = matches_won / total_matches
  ) |>
  filter(total_matches >= 5) |>
  arrange(desc(win_rate)) |>
  slice_max(order_by = win_rate, with_ties = TRUE)
total_matches
```

Rafael Nadal had the highest win rate, about 87%. 

Problem 3 - Visualization 
```{r}
#https://github.com/nytimes/covid-19-data/tree/master/rolling-averages
  #cases_avg: avg num of new cases reported over the most recent 7 days of data
us_states <- read.csv("us-states.csv")
head(us_states)
#unique(us_states$state)
```

a. How many major and minor spikes in cases were there?
```{r}
#https://www.r-bloggers.com/2023/11/getting-started-with-theme/

#tried just raw data, plot wasn't clear enough
  #use 7 day averages instead
us_states_a <- us_states |>
  group_by(date) |>
    #line idea from um-gpt
  summarize(cases_avg = sum(cases_avg)) |>
  ungroup()

plot_a <- us_states_a |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = as.Date(date), y = cases_avg)) + 
  geom_line(color = "darkblue") + 
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "5 months", date_labels = "%b\n%Y") + 
  #https://stackoverflow.com/questions/14563989/force-r-to-stop-plotting-abbreviated-axis-labels-scientific-notation-e-g-1e
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) + 
  labs(title = "New Covid-19 Cases in the U.S.", 
       x = "Date", y = "New Cases per Day (National 7-day Avg)") + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    #makes the axes more visible 
    axis.line = element_line(colour = "grey20"),
    #gets rid of the minor grid lines for cleaner look
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    #modify font
    text = element_text(family = "serif"),
    #adjust plot title
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 17),
    #pushes y axis label to the left
    axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(r = 10)),
    #pushes x axis label down
    axis.title.x = element_text(margin = margin(t = 10)),
    #add more space around edges of plot
    plot.margin = margin(t = 20, r = 20, b = 15, l = 15)
  )
plot_a 
```

There seems to be one major spike between about December 2021 and March 2022. 
Aside from this very clear spike, there's 3 minor spikes from November 2020 to 
February 2021, August 2021 to November 2021, and May 2022-September 2022. 

b. For the states with the highest and lowest overall rates per population, 
what differences do you see in their trajectories over time?
```{r}
not_states <- c("District of Columbia", "Puerto Rico", "Guam", "Virgin Islands",
            "Northern Mariana Islands", "American Samoa")

states_only <- us_states |>
  #keep states only
  filter(!(state %in% not_states))

#assuming cases_avg_per_100k is rate per popul (based on github) 
us_states_b <- states_only |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarize(overall_rate = sum(cases_avg_per_100k)) |>
  arrange(desc(overall_rate)) |>
  ungroup()
head(us_states_b)
#unique(us_states_b$state) #just to check

highest_overall_rate <- us_states_b |>
  slice_max(order_by = overall_rate)

lowest_overall_rate <- us_states_b |>
  slice_min(order_by = overall_rate)

#just get the states' names for plotting
rates <- c(highest_overall_rate$state, lowest_overall_rate$state)
rates

plot_b <- states_only |>
  filter(state %in% rates) |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = as.Date(date), 
                       y = cases_avg_per_100k, color = state)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  scale_x_date(name = NULL, date_breaks = "5 months", date_labels = "%b\n%Y") +
  labs(title = "New Covid-19 Cases for States with Highest/Lowest Overall Rate", 
       x = "Date", y = "New Cases per 100k People (7-day Avg) ") +
  scale_color_manual(name = NULL, values = c("violetred", "royalblue4")) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    #makes the axes more visible 
    axis.line = element_line(colour = "grey20"),
    #gets rid of the minor grid lines for cleaner look
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    #modify font
    text = element_text(family = "serif"),
    #adjust plot title
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 15),
    #pushes y axis label to the left
    axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(r = 10)),
    #pushes x axis label down
    axis.title.x = element_text(margin = margin(t = 10)),
    #add more space around edges of plot
    plot.margin = margin(t = 20, r = 20, b = 15, l = 15), 
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
plot_b
```

Rhode Island had the highest overall rate, and Maine had the lowest. The differ 
mostly in periods where Rhode Island experiences an increase in the average 
number of new cases while Maine stays relatively constant, or experiences a 
smaller increase. For example, between about December 2021 and March 2022, 
Rhode Island experiences a huge spike in the average number of new cases, while
Maine's numbers are mostly constant. 

c. Identify, to the best of your ability without a formal test, 
the first five states to experience Covid in a substantial way.
```{r}
#first date each state reached 25 new daily cases per 100,000 people
first_five <- states_only |>
  filter(cases_avg_per_100k >= 25) |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarize(first_date = min(date)) |>
  arrange(first_date) |>
  ungroup() |>
  slice_head(n = 5)
first_five

#beginning of pandemic (for plotting) (checked when cases started increasing)
pandemic_start <- states_only |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("2020-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2020-05-30"))

plot_c <- pandemic_start|>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = as.Date(date), y = cases_avg_per_100k)) +
  #grey lines for every state
  geom_line(aes(group = state), color = "grey80") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 25, color = "grey50") + 
  #colored lines on top for the first five states
  geom_line(data = filter(pandemic_start, state %in% first_five$state),
            aes(color = state), linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 week", date_labels = "%b %d") +
  labs(title = "First 5 States to Experience 25 New Cases per 100k People", 
       x = "Date", y = "New Cases per 100k People (7-day Avg)", 
       subtitle = "Grey horizontal line: 25 new daily cases per 100k") +
  scale_color_discrete(name = "First Five States", breaks = first_five$state) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  theme(
    #makes the axes more visible 
    axis.line = element_line(colour = "grey10"),
    #gets rid of the minor grid lines for cleaner look
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    #modify font
    text = element_text(family = "serif"),
    #adjust plot title
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 15),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 9),
    #pushes y axis label to the left
    axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(r = 10)),
    #pushes x axis label down
    axis.title.x = element_text(margin = margin(t = 10)),
    #add more space around edges of plot
    plot.margin = margin(t = 20, r = 20, b = 15, l = 15), 
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
plot_c
```

The first five states to experience Covid in a substantial way, which I defined 
as reaching a 7-day average of at least 25 new cases per 100k people, were 
New York, New Jersey, Louisiana, Connecticut, and Massachusetts.
